Who is your favorite science fiction writer?

I read Solaris as a kid (my dad was a sci-fi fan) and it was terrifying. Good stuff.

I have seen the Tarkovsky movie as a kid and resaw it not too long ago. That reminds me of the Strugatsky brothers, who wrote Roadside Picnic, which was also turned into a movie by Tarkovsky, as Stalker

The genre was infiltrated .. just as the 911 attacks were presaged in numerous television shows, in movies and on record sleeves, so were the major science fiction fan mags which fueled the explosion of SF literature in the early 1960's, used to presage future developments.

Including the computer age and the development of the internet .. one story caught my eye that was published in Analog Science Fiction, concerned a lone astronaut who had returned to Earth after a pioneering trip to Mars.

He described millions of dead bodies surrounding various lakes and seas, whereas living Martians dwelt at the shorelines and ate seaweed that washed up on the tides, until they in their turn succumbed and were trodden underfoot by the next generation..

Which has credence in the NASA Rover shots that reveal a vast volume of skulls on the Martian plain, which begs the conclusion manned missions to Mars had been undertaken by that time.

A lot of the stories were very engaging A.E. van Vogt, Robert A. Heinlein, Frederik Pohl, Joe Haldeman, Poul Anderson, Harry Harrison, Lester del Rey, Clifford D. Simak and Roger Zelazny come to mind.

I'm currently writing a game which pulls inspiration from the pre-golden age classics like Jules Verne.

But if I'm going Sci-Fi I'm going hard Sci-Fi. Arthur C. Clarke is the undisputed king.

Honorable mention goes to Andy Weir for "The Martian". But it's too soon to put him in the ranks of Clarke. Maybe if Weir writes 20 more stories as good as "The Martian".
Well, while young, Michael Crichton (the books, not the movies). Later: Thomas Pynchon's Gravity's Rainbow probably classifies as Sci Fi, so that one.
I read Jurassic Park before it was made into a movie, and liked it a lot!
Dune, Frank Herbert. Very interesting political blurbs and parallels with religions and storyline.

By both quantity (that I read) and quality (my enjoyment) that's definitely Arthur C. Clarke.

On an emotional level, it is H.P. Lovecraft. (HPL is commonly described as a horror writer, but most of his stories are arguably science fiction as well.)

In my youth I read some Asimov stories (the Foundation and Galactic Empire series, and short stories) which I found fascinating as for the overal timeline, but I was somewhat underwhelmed with how he depicted the main characters; imho there was always an element of boredom at that level.

Since I read Heinlein's Orphans of the Sky I might have to rank him as my #1, because it found it a great read, and I like what I've read of him. But that isn't very much to be honest.

John Wyndham's Day of the Triffids and The Chrysalids are also great (especially the latter), but I sofar didn't read any other of his books.

I've read some of James Luceno's novels set in the Star Wars universe, and he's superb!

When I was younger, I read many of Michael Crichton's novels, and re-read some of them several times over. Into my twenties, I read a good bit of Orson Scott Card.

Favorite all time though, would have to go to Crichton.
